In mathematics, especially [[homotopy theory]], a '''cartesian fibration''' is, roughly, a map so that every lift exists that is a [[final object]] among all lifts. For example, the [[forgetful functor]]
:<math>\textrm{QCoh} \to \textrm{Sch}</math>
from the category of pairs <math>(X, F)</math> of [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]s and [[quasi-coherent sheaves]] on them is a cartesian fibration (see {{section link||Basic example}}). In fact, the [[Grothendieck construction]] says all cartesian fibrations are of this type; i.e., they simply forget extra data. See also: [[fibred category]], [[prestack]].

The dual of a cartesian fibration is called an '''op-fibration'''; in particular, not a cocartesian fibration.

A [[right fibration]] between [[simplicial set]]s is an example of a cartesian fibration.

== Definition ==
Given a functor <math>\pi : C \to S</math>, a morphism <math>f : x \to y</math> in <math>C</math> is called '''<math>\pi</math>-cartesian''' or simply '''cartesian''' if the natural map 
:<math>(f_*, \pi) : \operatorname{Hom}(z, x) \to \operatorname{Hom}(z, y) \times_{\operatorname{Hom}(\pi(z), \pi(y))} \operatorname{Hom}(\pi(z), \pi(x))</math>
is bijective.<ref>{{harvnb|Kerodon|loc=Definition 5.0.0.1.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Khan|2022|loc=Definition 3.1.1.}}</ref> Explicitly, thus, <math>f : x \to y</math> is cartesian if given
*<math>g: z \to y</math> and
*<math>u : \pi(z) \to \pi(x)</math>
with <math>\pi(g) = \pi(f) \circ u</math>, there exists a unique <math>g' : z \to x</math> in <math>\pi^{-1}(u)</math> such that <math>f \circ g' = g</math>.

Then <math>\pi</math> is called a cartesian fibration if for each morphism of the form <math>f : s \to \pi(z)</math> in ''S'', there exists a <math>\pi</math>-cartesian morphism <math>g : a \to z</math> in ''C'' such that <math>\pi(g) = f</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Khan|2022|loc=Definition 3.1.2.}}</ref> Here, the object <math>a</math> is unique up to unique isomorphisms (if <math>b \to z</math> is another lift, there is a unique <math>b \to a</math>, which is shown to be an isomorphism). Because of this, the object <math>a</math> is often thought of as the pullback of <math>z</math> and is sometimes even denoted as <math>f^* z</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Vistoli|2008|loc=Definition 3.1. and § 3.1.2.}}</ref> Also, somehow informally, <math>g</math> is said to be a [[final object]] among all lifts of <math>f</math>.

A morphism <math>\varphi : \pi \to \rho</math> between cartesian fibrations over the same base ''S'' is a map (functor) over the base; i.e., <math>\pi = \rho \circ \varphi</math> that sends cartesian morphisms to cartesian morphisms.<ref>{{harvnb|Vistoli|2008|loc=Definition 3.6.}}</ref> Given <math>\varphi, \psi : \pi \to \rho</math>, a 2-morphism <math>\theta : \varphi \rightarrow \psi</math> is an invertible map (map = [[natural transformation]]) such that for each object <math>E</math> in the source of <math>\pi</math>, <math>\theta_E : \varphi(E) \to \psi(E)</math> maps to the [[Identity function|identity map]] of the object <math>\rho(\varphi(E)) = \rho(\psi(E))</math> under <math>\rho</math>.

This way, all the cartesian fibrations over the fixed base category ''S'' determine the [[(2, 1)-category]] denoted by <math>\operatorname{Cart}(S)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Khan|2022|loc=Construction 3.1.4.}}</ref>

== Basic example ==
Let <math>\operatorname{QCoh}</math> be the category where
*an object is a pair <math>(X, F)</math> of a scheme <math>X</math> and a quasi-coherent sheaf <math>F</math> on it,
*a morphism <math>\overline{f} : (X, F) \to (Y, G)</math> consists of a morphism <math>f : X \to Y</math> of schemes and a sheaf homomorphism <math>\varphi_f : f^* G \overset{\sim}\to F</math> on <math>X</math>,
*the composition <math>\overline{g} \circ \overline{f}</math> of <math>\overline{g} : (Y, G) \to (Z, H)</math> and above <math>\overline{f}</math> is the (unique) morphism <math>\overline{h}</math> such that <math>h = g \circ f</math> and <math>\varphi_h</math> is
*:<math>(g \circ f)^*H \simeq f^* g^* H \overset{f^*\varphi_g}\to f^*G \overset{\varphi_f}\to F.</math>
To see the forgetful map
:<math>\pi : \operatorname{QCoh} \to \operatorname{Sch}</math>
is a cartesian fibration,<ref>{{harvnb|Khan|2022|loc=Example 3.1.3.}}</ref> let <math>f : X \to \pi((Y, G))</math> be in <math>\operatorname{QCoh}</math>. Take
:<math>\overline{f} = (f, \varphi_f) : (X, F) \to (Y, G)</math>
with <math>F = f^* G</math> and <math>\varphi_f = \operatorname{id}</math>. We claim <math>\overline{f}</math> is cartesian. Given <math>\overline{g} : (Z, H) \to (Y, G)</math> and <math>h : Z \to X</math> with <math>g = f \circ h</math>, if <math>\varphi_h</math> exists such that <math>\overline{g} = \overline{f} \circ \overline{h}</math>, then we have <math>\varphi_g</math> is
:<math>(f \circ h)^* G \simeq h^* f^* G = h^* F \overset{\varphi_h}\to H.</math>
So, the required <math>\overline{h}</math> trivially exists and is unique.

Note some authors consider <math>\operatorname{QCoh}^{\simeq}</math>, the [[core of a category|core]] of <math>\operatorname{QCoh}</math> instead. In that case, the forgetful map restricted to it is also a cartesian fibration.

== Grothendieck construction ==
{{main|Grothendieck construction}}

Given a category <math>S</math>, the Grothendieck construction gives an equivalence of ∞-categories between <math>\operatorname{Cart}(S)</math> and the ∞-category of [[prestack]]s on <math>S</math> (prestacks = category-valued presheaves).<ref>{{harvnb|Khan|2022|loc=Theorem 3.1.5.}}</ref>

Roughly, the construction goes as follows: given a cartesian fibration <math>\pi</math>, we let <math>F_{\pi} : S^{op} \to \textbf{Cat}</math> be the map that sends each object ''x'' in ''S'' to the fiber <math>\pi^{-1}(x)</math>. So, <math>F_{\pi}</math> is a <math>\textbf{Cat}</math>-valued presheaf or a prestack. Conversely, given a prestack <math>F</math>, define the category <math>C_F</math> where an object is a pair <math>(x, a)</math> with <math>a \in F(x)</math> and then let <math>\pi</math> be the forgetful functor to <math>S</math>. Then these two assignments give the claimed equivalence.

For example, if the construction is applied to the forgetful <math>\pi : \textrm{QCoh} \to \textrm{Sch}</math>, then we get the map <math>X \mapsto \textrm{QCoh}(X)</math> that sends a scheme <math>X</math> to the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on <math>X</math>. Conversely, <math>\pi</math> is determined by such a map.

[[Lurie's straightening theorem]] generalizes the above equivalence to the equivalence between the ∞-category of cartesian fibrations over some ∞-category ''C'' and the ∞-category of ∞-prestacks on ''C''.<ref>An introduction in Louis Martini, Cocartesian fibrations and straightening internal to an ∞-topos [arXiv:2204.00295]</ref>
